title: Solubility based mechanistic profiling of combinatorial drug therapy
projectDescription: Acute myeloid leukemia (AML) poses a major clinical challenge due to its genetic diversity, relapse rates, and chemotherapy toxicity. While rational drug combinations improve efficacy, their mechanisms remain poorly understood. We introduce CoPISA (Proteome Integral Solubility/Stability Alteration Analysis for Combinations), a high-throughput proteomics workflow that identifies protein solubility/stability changes unique to drug combinations.  Applied to two AML drug pairs—LY3009120-sapanisertib (LS) and ruxolitinib-ulixertinib (RU)—CoPISA mapped protein targets in lysates and living cells. The analysis revealed a novel principle, “conjunctional targeting”, where drug pairs induce unique, cooperative effects not seen with individual drugs, akin to an AND-gate logic. LS-specific targets involved SUMOylation, chromatin condensation, and VEGF-linked adhesion; RU-specific targets disrupted DNA damage checkpoints, mitochondrial function, and RNA splicing, suggesting synthetic-lethal vulnerabilities.  Post-translational modification profiling confirmed combination-induced changes (e.g., acetylation, dimethylation, phosphorylation) on key AML proteins like NPM1. Network analysis showed many targets were unique to combinations, including frequently mutated drivers DNMT3A, NPM1, and TP53. CoPISA reveals how drug pairs exert multi-axis pressure on AML cells, offering a mechanistic layer beyond classical synergy and guiding precision therapy design for AML and other complex cancers.
sampleProcessingProtocol: Protein concentrations were determined using the Pierce BCA Protein Assay Kit (Thermo). From each sample, 27 μg of protein was transferred to Amicon Ultra-0.5 mL 10KD centrifugal filter tubes. Volumes were equalized with 20 mM EPPS buffer, followed by reduction with 10 mM DTT (55 °C, 30 min) and alkylation with 50 mM iodoacetamide (25 °C, 60 min, dark). Samples were centrifuged (14,000 g, 20 min) and washed twice with EPPS buffer. Proteins were digested overnight at 37 °C with trypsin (1:50 ratio) under vigorous shaking. Peptides were collected by centrifugation and rinsing with EPPS. The resulting peptides were collected by centrifugation and rinsing the filter tubes with EPPS. Prior to labeling, equal amounts of each sample from the different treatment groups were mixed for separate labeling. A total of 25 μg from each sample was labeled using tandem mass tags (TMT) according to the manufacturer’s protocol (Thermo Fisher Scientific). Three technical replicates for each treatment (drug A, drug B, AB, and control), along with one mixed sample of each condition, were pooled together, resulting in a final mixture of 325 μg from 13 samples.  TMT-labeled peptides were fractionated using high-pH reversed-phase chromatography on an XBridge Peptide BEH C18 column (1 mm × 150 mm, 3.5 µm, 130 Å; Waters) with an Ultimate 3000 system (Thermo). Peptides were loaded in 20 mM ammonium formate (pH 10, Solution A) and separated using a gradient from 2% to 80% Solution B (20 mM ammonium formate in 90% acetonitrile, pH 10) over 75 min at 42 µL/min. UV detection was performed at 205 and 214 nm. Thirty-six fractions were collected and concatenated into 12 pools, then dried under vacuum.  Dried peptides were resuspended in 0.1% formic acid and analyzed on an Orbitrap Eclipse Tribrid Mass Spectrometer with an Ultimate 3000 nanoLC system, FAIMS Pro interface, and a 60 °C column heater. Peptides were separated on a 75 μm × 30 cm in-house packed C18 column (1.9 μm ReproSil-Pur C18–AQ) at 0.3 μL/min using a gradient from 2% to 95% acetonitrile (0.1% formic acid) over 110 min.  The instrument operated in data-dependent acquisition (DDA) mode with a 3 s cycle time. FAIMS CVs alternated between −40 V and −70 V every 1.5 s. MS1 scans were acquired in the Orbitrap (120,000 resolution, 400–1600 m/z, AGC target “Standard”, max injection time “Auto”). Precursors (charge 2–6, intensity >5e3) were isolated (0.7 m/z window), dynamically excluded for 45 s, and fragmented via CID (30% energy). MS2 spectra were acquired in the ion trap at “Turbo” scan rate.  MS2 spectra were searched in real-time against a human UniProt database (20,362 entries, downloaded 2020-04-17). Search parameters: trypsin enzyme, fixed modifications (TMTpro16plex on K/N-term, carbamidomethyl on C), variable oxidation (M), max 1 missed cleavage, 2 variable mods, 100 ms max search time, 1.4 XCorr, 0.1 dCn, 10 ppm precursor tolerance, charge state 2, and “TMT SPS MS3 Mode” enabled.  Filtered spectra (400–1600 m/z) excluded precursors ±25 ppm and TMTpro tag loss. MS3 scans were triggered for identified precursors using a 2 m/z isolation window, 200 ms max injection time, AGC target 200%, and HCD fragmentation (55% energy). MS3 spectra were acquired in the Orbitrap (50,000 resolution, 100–500 m/z) with SPS enabled (10 precursors).
dataProcessingProtocol: The acquired raw files were analyzed using the MaxQuant software (v2.6.5.0). Spectra were searched against a human protein sequences database (downloaded from Uniprot on 20241010). Group-specific parameters were used as follows. The type of the search was set to Reporter MS3. Isobaric labels and their correction factors were provided according to the manufacturer kit sheet. Normalization was set to a weighted ratio to the reference channel. Variable modifications were set to oxidation of methionines and acetylation of N-termini, while fixed modification settings contained only carbamidomethylation of cysteines. The maximum number of modifications per peptide was set to 3. Two missed cleavages with Trypsin/P were allowed. For the refined search, all settings were kept as in the original with the addition of variable modifications as proposed by the PEIMAN2 R package, with five as a maximum number of modifications per peptide.
